program_meta.program_name: Ph.D. in Computer Science (CS division) — Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Sciences (EECS), College of Engineering. NOTE THE DIVISION SPLIT: EECS runs two separate degrees. On the Graduate Division application, the EE division is listed as 'Electrical Engineering and Computer Sciences (EECS)' and the CS division is listed as 'Computer Science (CS)'. VERBATIM from the EECS admissions page: 'EE applicants must make sure to apply to EECS, and CS applicants make sure to apply to CS.' For Akshat the correct target is the CS division, area 'Artificial Intelligence (AI)' (or 'CS: AI-SCIENCE' if he leads with Krishnapriyan/Listgarten — both of them explicitly instruct EECS applicants to select AI-SCIENCE as primary area). Adjacent non-EECS routes worth noting: the Statistics Ph.D. (Song Mei, Bin Yu, Ryan Tibshirani, Adam Yala, Jacob Steinhardt all sit partly or wholly there), the Center for Computational Biology, and Bioengineering.
program_meta.sop_limit: NO HARD LIMIT — this is stated explicitly, twice, and is unusual enough to be worth planning around. VERBATIM from the EECS Graduate Admissions FAQ ('What is the difference between the Statement of Purpose and Personal History Statement? How long should each essay be?'): 'There is no minimum or maximum length requirement for either essay. Though many applicants aim for each essay to be between 500-1000 words or 1-2 pages. It's okay if there is a little overlap of information between the SOP and PHS.' The Graduate Division's own writing guide adds, VERBATIM: 'Unless the specific program says otherwise, be concise; an ideal essay should say everything it needs to with brevity. Approximately 500 to 1,000 well-selected words is better than more words with less clarity and poor organization.' PRACTICAL TARGET: 900-1,000 words for the SOP. The Graduate Division SOP prompt is, VERBATIM: 'Please describe your aptitude and motivation for graduate study in your area of specialization, including your preparation for this field of study, your academic plans or research interests, and your future career goals. Please be specific about why UC Berkeley would be a good intellectual fit for you.' That last sentence is a direct instruction to name faculty and labs.
program_meta.extra_essays: YES — a separate Personal History Statement (PHS) is REQUIRED of every Berkeley applicant, university-wide, and is submitted alongside the SOP. Length: same rule, no minimum or maximum, 500-1000 words / 1-2 pages typical. VERBATIM Graduate Division prompt: 'Please describe how your background and life experiences have influenced your decision to pursue a graduate degree at this time. This may include formative experiences, values, or motivations that have influenced your academic and/or professional path.' It also VERBATIM states: 'The Personal History statement should not duplicate the Statement of Purpose.' The EECS FAQ softens this slightly: 'It's okay if there is a little overlap of information between the SOP and PHS.' The Graduate Division prompt invites (optionally) discussion of educational/familial/cultural/economic/social experiences, barriers overcome, leadership and community/outreach work, and alignment with UC Berkeley's Principles of Community. FOR AKSHAT: the PHS is the natural home for the 16-person autonomous go-kart team lead, the co-founded MedTech startup, and any account of doing research at a young institute without a large lab infrastructure — keep all of that OUT of the SOP so the SOP stays technical. NO OTHER SUPPLEMENTAL FORM EXISTS. VERBATIM EECS FAQ: 'No, we do not have a supplemental application. Applicants only need to complete the university graduate application.' A resume/CV is required.

program_meta.english_test: REQUIRED FOR AKSHAT — THERE IS NO INDIA EXEMPTION. The Graduate Division's country table lists, VERBATIM: 'Country of Undergraduate Institution: India | TOEFL/IELTS Required: Yes', with no institutional carve-outs (contrast Hong Kong, Turkey, Lebanon, UAE, Egypt, Armenia, Germany and Hungary, which all have named exceptions; India does not). This is a HARD DIFFERENCE from UT Austin, where India IS on the qualifying-countries list — Akshat cannot reuse that assumption. The only exemption routes are: a degree from a country where English is the primary language of daily life and instruction; a degree from a U.S. or U.S.-abroad accredited institution; or one year of full-time coursework with grades of B or better at a U.S. regionally accredited institution. None apply. MINIMUMS FOR FALL 2027 ENTRY: TOEFL iBT (or iBT Home Edition) — tests taken 1 June 2025 to 20 January 2026 need a 90 minimum total; tests taken on or after 21 January 2026 need, VERBATIM, '5 minimum total score, with 4.5 minimum Speaking and Writing section scores' (this is the redesigned 1-6 TOEFL band scale, not the 120 scale — verify against ETS before booking). IELTS Academic — 7.0 overall for tests 1 June 2025 to 20 January 2026; 7.0 overall with 6.5 minimum Speaking and Writing for tests on or after 21 January 2026. Tests taken BEFORE 1 JUNE 2025 WILL NOT BE ACCEPTED for Fall 2027 even if already reported to Berkeley. NOT accepted at all: Duolingo, TOEFL ITP, TOEFL MyBest Scores, IELTS Indicator, IELTS One Test Retake. TOEFL institution code 4833 (Graduate Organizations); IELTS needs no code and must be sent electronically from the test centre. EECS advises taking the test 'by November'. Departments may set a higher bar than the campus minimum.

program_meta.advisor_model: DEPARTMENT ADMISSION with a faculty-of-interest field — you do NOT need a pre-arranged advisor, and cold-emailing is explicitly declared unnecessary. VERBATIM, EECS Graduate Admissions FAQ, question 'Do I need to contact faculty or establish an advisor before I apply?': 'No, you do not need to contact faulty or establish an advisor in order to apply. Instead, on the application, you will list faculty members who you would like to work with should you be admitted to our graduate program. You can view the list of all our current faculty or you can view the faculty associated with each research area.' (The typo 'faulty' is Berkeley's.) STRATEGIC READING: this is the single most important line in this file. Berkeley has closed the cold-email channel at the departmental level, so the faculty-of-interest list plus the 'why UC Berkeley would be a good intellectual fit' sentence in the SOP are the ONLY levers Akshat has. Several individual faculty reinforce it in stronger language (Levine and Malik both tell prospective students not to contact them; Krishnapriyan says she cannot reply). Two named professors additionally instruct EECS applicants to select the 'CS: AI-SCIENCE' primary area (Krishnapriyan, Listgarten). Berkeley EECS has no rotation system; students are matched to advisors after arrival. Ph.D. length is stated as 5-6 years starting from a bachelor's. ONE APPLICATION ONLY — VERBATIM: 'No, you can only submit one graduate school application per admission cycle.' So Akshat must choose EECS-CS vs Statistics vs Computational Biology up front and cannot hedge.
program_meta.ms_research_access: MIXED — and the useful master's route is CLOSED to him. (1) 5th YEAR M.S.: NOT AVAILABLE. VERBATIM from the EECS industry-programs comparison page: 'Berkeley undergraduates only... This program is for Berkeley EECS/CDSS CS undergraduates only and requires a continued research project with an EECS faculty member. It is not intended for students who have definitely decided to pursue a Ph.D.' It is a one-year, full-time, research-continuation degree with a mid-December deadline — genuine lab access, but you must already be a Berkeley undergraduate, so Akshat is ineligible. (2) M.Eng.: essentially NO research access. It is a one-year professional degree built around technical courses plus an engineering-leadership curriculum and a TEAM-BASED CAPSTONE PROJECT sourced from the Fung Capstone Marketplace each August — an industry-sponsored group project, not a thesis and not a lab placement. Admissions rate ~12%; deadline 14 January; TOEFL iBT 90 minimum. Do not treat M.Eng. as a PhD on-ramp. (3) RESEARCH M.S. (M.S.-only): technically research-bearing but effectively closed. VERBATIM: 'The MS only degree is intended mostly for currently registered UC Berkeley Ph.D. students that want to add the degree. Occasionally we admit exceptional applicants with research experience, but the cohort generally is limited to less than 10. Students interested in a research oriented degree should consider applying directly to the MS/PhD program.' (4) M.S./Ph.D.: the correct research route for an external applicant who wants a master's on the way to the doctorate. CONCLUSION FOR AKSHAT: apply Ph.D. or M.S./Ph.D. in the CS division. There is no viable terminal-master's back door into a Berkeley lab. Note also: 'The EECS Department does not allow part-time study for the MS or PhD programs' and 'all of our graduate programs are on campus.'

faculty.department: Computational Precision Health (joint UC Berkeley / UCSF); Statistics; Electrical Engineering and Computer Sciences
faculty.lab: Yala Lab (Berkeley-UCSF); affiliated with Computational Precision Health (CPH)
faculty.research_areas: Machine learning for personalized health care and clinical translation; cancer risk prediction from imaging (mammography); learned screening and treatment policies; modelling full multi-modal patient records including imaging and vision-language; decision guarantees for AI-driven predictors; radiology and oncology deployment
faculty.why_match: Akshat's semi-supervised lumbar-spine result is the exact problem Yala's group is now attacking at CT scale: a U-Net teacher trained on 54 labelled SPIDER images reached 0.735 mIoU, and filtering its pseudo-labels by per-class confidence lifted a student to 0.816 mIoU, +8.1 absolute points, with the further finding that thresholds calibrated on only 5 reference images matched those calibrated on 304. Yala is a co-author on 'Open-Ended CT Volume Segmentation with Weak Supervision from Language' (arXiv:2607.25860, 2026), which replaces dense voxel annotation with language-derived weak supervision on CT volumes — the same annotation-scarcity bottleneck, attacked from the supervision side rather than the pseudo-label side. Akshat's calibration-efficiency result (5 reference images suffice) is directly usable as a filtering criterion inside that kind of weakly supervised pipeline, and his DDPM pretraining study on BTCV abdominal CT (liver Dice 0.751 to 0.928, frozen encoder retaining 86.9% of the fine-tuned liver Dice but COLLAPSING on kidney to 0.654, below the 0.899 random-init baseline) is a per-structure transferability question posed on exactly the CT anatomy Yala's group is segmenting.

faculty.department: Electrical Engineering and Computer Sciences (CS and EE divisions)
faculty.lab: Darrell Group; Founding Co-Director of Berkeley Artificial Intelligence Research (BAIR), Berkeley DeepDrive (BDD) and BAIR Commons
faculty.research_areas: Large-scale perceptual learning; weakly and image-level supervised detection and segmentation; constrained output spaces; domain adaptation; vision-language models and multimodal alignment; video and embodied perception; autonomous driving
faculty.why_match: HiME's contribution is that hierarchy consistency is a property of the DECODING RULE, not a measured number: per-level conditional sigmoids composed by the chain rule bound each child's probability by its parent's, so the prediction set is upward-closed by construction, verified as consistency 1.000 across five backbones on Galaxy Zoo 2 (239,573 images, 37 classes, 4 levels, 95.8% decision-level accuracy) at roughly 0.01% parameter overhead. Darrell co-authored 'Constrained Convolutional Neural Networks for Weakly Supervised Segmentation' (Pathak, Krähenbühl, Darrell; ICCV 2015), which makes precisely that move — express supervision as linear constraints on the output label distribution instead of relying on dense labels — and does it in Akshat's own modality. The live continuation of that line is 'Open-Ended CT Volume Segmentation with Weak Supervision from Language' (arXiv:2607.25860, 2026), on which Darrell is a co-author with Adam Yala and Dan Klein, and which sits directly on top of Akshat's SPIDER pseudo-labelling result (54 labelled images, teacher 0.735 mIoU, filtered-pseudo-label student 0.816 mIoU) and his MoNuSeg nucleus-segmentation work. Interests A and C meet inside one group, and Akshat's go-kart perception stack (ROS 2, LiDAR-camera fusion, 56 FPS segmentation) maps onto Berkeley DeepDrive.

faculty.lab: Efros Research Group; Berkeley Artificial Intelligence Research (BAIR)
faculty.research_areas: Self-supervised and data-driven visual representation learning; generative image models and what pretext tasks actually teach; test-time training and continual learning; dataset bias, data attribution and evaluation methodology; computational photography; world models
faculty.why_match: Efros's stated central goal is, VERBATIM, 'to use vast amounts of unlabelled visual data to understand, model, and recreate the visual world around us', and he dates his own self-supervised learning line to 2015 — that is Akshat's interest B stated as a research programme. Two of his recent papers map onto specific unresolved results in Akshat's work. First, 'The FID Lottery: Quantifying Hidden Randomness in Generative-Model Evaluation' (N. Dufour, A. A. Efros, P. Pérez; arXiv:2606.20536, 2026) is exactly the methodological problem that undermines Akshat's own numbers: his DDPM-pretraining study on BTCV ran a single seed on one NVIDIA A2000, and his polyp result won by 0.0049 Dice, a margin smaller than plausible seed noise. Second, 'Visual Jenga: Discovering object dependencies via counterfactual inpainting' (A. Bhattad, K. Preechakul, A. A. Efros; NeurIPS 2025) uses a generative model as a probe to find out what structure it has actually internalised — which is precisely the untested hypothesis in Akshat's diffusion paper, where the frozen encoder retained 86.9% of the fine-tuned liver Dice but scored 0.654 on kidney against a 0.899 random-init baseline. Akshat's per-organ transfer split is stated but never explained; counterfactual probing of a diffusion prior is a concrete way to explain it.

faculty.rank: CDSS Chancellor's Professor and Chair, Department of Statistics
faculty.research_areas: Distribution-free inference and conformal prediction; probabilistic and calibrated forecasting; high-dimensional statistics; nonparametric estimation; convex optimisation and numerical methods; computational epidemiology
faculty.why_match: Akshat's SPIDER pipeline turns entirely on a filtering threshold, and he swept it empirically: per-class optimal thresholds lifted pseudo-label IoU from 0.7437 to 0.8529; a fixed global threshold of 0.98 reached 0.9377 IoU but discarded roughly 17% of pixels; MC-dropout uncertainty was comparable (0.7910-0.7922) and combining it with confidence added nothing. Every one of those numbers is a hand-tuned heuristic standing in for a coverage guarantee. Tibshirani's 'Class-Conditional Conformal Prediction with Many Classes' (T. Ding, A. Angelopoulos, S. Bates, M. Jordan, R. Tibshirani; NeurIPS 2023) supplies the principled replacement and does it in the many-class regime that HiME lives in — 37 classes across 4 levels on Galaxy Zoo 2, where HiME's guarantee is structural (upward-closed prediction sets by construction) but carries NO coverage statement at all. Pairing HiME's structural guarantee with a class-conditional conformal coverage guarantee is a well-posed, publishable question that neither side has done. 'Conformal Prediction Beyond Exchangeability' (Barber, Candès, Ramdas, Tibshirani; Annals of Statistics 2023) covers the case Akshat actually has: pseudo-labelled data is not exchangeable with the labelled seed set.
